{{Short description|Concept in group theory (mathematics)}}
{{Orphan|date=September 2024}}

The '''invariant decomposition''' is a decomposition of the elements of [[pin group]]s <math>\text{Pin}(p,q,r)</math> into orthogonal commuting elements. It is also valid in their subgroups, e.g. [[Orthogonal group|orthogonal]], [[Pseudo-Euclidean space|pseudo-Euclidean]], [[Conformal group|conformal]], and [[classical group]]s. Because the elements of [[Pin group]]s are the composition of <math>k</math> oriented reflections, the invariant decomposition theorem reads<blockquote>Every <math>k</math>-reflection can be decomposed into <math display="inline">\lceil k/2 \rceil</math> commuting factors.<ref name=":0">{{Cite web |last1=Roelfs |first1=Martin |last2=De Keninck |first2=Steven |title=Graded Symmetry Groups: Plane and Simple |url=https://www.researchgate.net/publication/353116859 }}</ref></blockquote>
It is named the invariant decomposition because these factors are the invariants of the <math>k</math>-reflection <math>R \in \text{Pin}(p,q,r)</math>. A well known special case is the [[Chasles' theorem (kinematics)|Chasles' theorem]], which states that any [[rigid body]] motion in <math display="inline">\text{SE}(3)</math> can be decomposed into a rotation around, followed or preceded by a translation along, a single line. Both the rotation and the translation leave two lines invariant: the axis of rotation and the orthogonal axis of translation. Since both rotations and translations are bireflections, a more abstract statement of the theorem reads "Every quadreflection can be decomposed into commuting bireflections". In this form the statement is also valid for e.g. the spacetime algebra <math display="inline">\text{SO}(3,1)</math>, where any [[Lorentz transformation]] can be decomposed into a commuting rotation and boost.

== Bivector decomposition ==
Any bivector <math>F</math> in the geometric algebra <math>\mathbb{R}_{p,q,r}</math> of total dimension <math>n = p+q+r</math> can be decomposed into <math>k = \lfloor n / 2 \rfloor</math> orthogonal commuting simple bivectors that satisfy

<math display="block">F = F_1 + F_2 \ldots + F_{k}.</math>

Defining <math>\lambda_i := F_i^2 \in \mathbb{C}</math>, their properties can be summarized as <math>F_i F_j = \delta_{ij} \lambda_i + F_i \wedge F_j</math> (no sum). The <math>F_i</math> are then found as solutions to the [[characteristic polynomial]]

<math display="block">
0 = (F_1 - F_i) (F_2 - F_i) \cdots (F_k - F_i).
</math>

Defining

<math display="block">W_{m} = \frac{1}{m!}\langle F^{m}\rangle_{2 m} = \frac{1}{m!}\, \underbrace{F \wedge F \wedge \ldots \wedge F}_{m\ \text{times}}
</math>and <math>r = \lfloor k/2 \rfloor</math>, the solutions are given by

<math display="block">F_i
= \begin{cases}
\dfrac{\lambda_i^{r} W_0 + \lambda_i^{r-1} W_2 + \ldots + W_k}{\lambda_i^{r-1} W_1 + \lambda_i^{r-2} W_3 + \ldots + W_{k-1}} \quad & k \text{ even}, \\[10mu]
\dfrac{\lambda_i^{r} W_1 + \lambda_i^{r-1} W_3 + \ldots + W_k}{\lambda_i^{r}  W_0  + \lambda_i^{r-1} W_2 + \ldots + W_{k-1}} & k \text{ odd}.
\end{cases}</math>

The values of <math>\lambda_i</math> are subsequently found by squaring this expression and rearranging, which yields the polynomial

<math display="block">\begin{aligned}
0 &= \sum_{m=0}^{k} \langle W_{m}^2 \rangle_0 (- \lambda_i)^{k-m} \\[5mu]
&= (F_1^2 - \lambda_i) (F_2^2 - \lambda_i) \cdots (F_k^2 - \lambda_i).
\end{aligned}</math>

By allowing complex values for <math>\lambda_i</math>, the counter example of Marcel Riesz can in fact be solved.<ref name=":0" /> This closed form solution for the invariant decomposition is only valid for eigenvalues <math>\lambda_i</math> with algebraic multiplicity of 1. For degenerate <math>\lambda_i</math> the invariant decomposition still exists, but cannot be found using the closed form solution.

== Exponential map ==
A <math>2k</math>-reflection <math>R \in \text{Spin}(p,q,r)</math> can be written as <math>R = \exp(F)</math> where <math>F \in \mathfrak{spin}(p,q,r)</math> is a bivector, and thus permits a factorization

<math display="block">
R = e^F = e^{F_1} e^{F_2} \cdots e^{F_k}.
</math>

The invariant decomposition therefore gives a closed form formula for exponentials, since each <math>F_i</math> squares to a scalar and thus follows Euler's formula:

<math display="block">
R_i = e^{F_i} =
{\cosh}\bigl(\sqrt{\lambda_i}\bigr)
  + \frac{{\sinh}\bigl(\sqrt{\lambda_i}\bigr)}{\sqrt{\lambda_i}} F_i.
</math>

Carefully evaluating the limit <math>\lambda_i \to 0</math> gives

<math display="block">R_i = e^{F_i} = 1 + F_i,</math>

and thus translations are also included.

== Rotor factorization ==
Given a <math>2k</math>-reflection <math>R \in \text{Spin}(p,q,r)</math> we would like to find the factorization into <math>R_i = \exp(F_i)</math>. Defining the simple bivector

<math display="block">
t(F_i) := \frac{{\tanh}\bigl(\sqrt{\lambda_i}\bigr)}{\sqrt{\lambda_i}} F_i,
</math>

where <math>\lambda_i = F_i^2</math>. These bivectors can be found directly using the above solution for bivectors by substituting<ref name=":0" />

<math display="block">W_m = \langle R \rangle_{2m} \big/ \langle R \rangle_0</math>

where <math>\langle R \rangle_{2m}</math> selects the grade <math>2m</math> part of <math>R</math>. After the bivectors <math>t(F_i)</math> have been found, <math>R_i</math> is found straightforwardly as

<math display="block">R_i = \frac{1 + t(F_i)}{\sqrt{1 - t(F_i)^2}}.</math>

== Principal logarithm ==
After the decomposition of <math>R \in \text{Spin}(p,q,r)</math> into <math>R_i = \exp(F_i)</math> has been found, the principal logarithm of each simple rotor is given by

<math display="block">F_i = \text{Log}(R_i) = \begin{cases}
\dfrac{\langle R_i \rangle_2 }{\textstyle \sqrt{\langle R_i \rangle\vphantom)_2^2}} \;\text{arccosh}(\langle R_i \rangle) \quad & \lambda_i^2 \neq 0, \\[5mu]
\langle R_i \rangle_2 & \lambda_i^2 = 0.
\end{cases}</math>

and thus the logarithm of <math>R</math> is given by

<math display="block">\text{Log}(R) = \sum_{i=1}^k \text{Log}(R_i).</math>

== General Pin group elements ==
So far we have only considered elements of <math>\text{Spin}(p,q,r)</math>, which are <math>2k</math>-reflections. To extend the invariant decomposition to a <math>(2k+1)</math>-reflections <math>P \in \text{Pin}(p,q,r)</math>, we use that the vector part <math>r = \langle P \rangle_1</math> is a reflection which already commutes with, and is orthogonal to, the <math>2k</math>-reflection <math>R = r^{-1} P = P r^{-1}</math>. The problem then reduces to finding the decomposition of <math>R</math> using the method described above.

== Invariant bivectors ==
The bivectors <math>F_i</math> are invariants of the corresponding <math>R \in \text{Spin}(p,q,r)</math> since they commute with it, and thus under group conjugation

<math display="block">R F_i R^{-1} = F_i.</math>

Going back to the example of [[Chasles' theorem (kinematics)|Chasles' theorem]] as given in the introduction, the screw motion in 3D leaves invariant the two lines <math>F_1</math> and <math>F_2</math>, which correspond to the axis of rotation and the orthogonal axis of translation on the horizon. While the entire space undergoes a screw motion, these two axes remain unchanged by it.

== History ==
The invariant decomposition finds its roots in a statement made by [[Marcel Riesz]] about [[bivector]]s:<ref>{{Cite book |last=Riesz |first=Marcel |editor-first1=E. Folke |editor-first2=Pertti |editor-last1=Bolinder |editor-last2=Lounesto |date=1993 |title=Clifford Numbers and Spinors |url=https://doi.org/10.1007/978-94-017-1047-3 |language=en-gb |doi=10.1007/978-94-017-1047-3|isbn=978-90-481-4279-8 }}</ref><blockquote>Can any bivector <math>F</math> be decomposed into the direct sum of mutually orthogonal simple bivectors?</blockquote>Mathematically, this would mean that for a given bivector <math>F</math> in an <math>n</math> dimensional [[geometric algebra]], it should be possible to find a maximum of <math display="inline">k = \lfloor n/2 \rfloor</math> bivectors <math>F_i</math>, such that <math display="inline">F = \sum_{i=1}^{\lfloor n/2 \rfloor} F_i</math>, where the <math>F_i</math> satisfy <math>F_i \cdot F_j = [F_i, F_j] = 0</math>  and should square to a scalar <math>\lambda_i := F_i^2 \in \mathbb{R}</math>. [[Marcel Riesz]] gave some examples which lead to this conjecture, but also one (seeming) counter example. A first more general solution to the conjecture in geometric algebras <math>\mathbb{R}_{n,0,0}</math> was given by [[David Hestenes]] and [[Garret Sobczyck]].<ref>{{Cite book |last=Hestenes |first=David |title=Clifford algebra to geometric calculus: a unified language for mathematics and physics |date=1984 |publisher=D. Reidel |others=Garret Sobczyk |isbn=90-277-1673-0 |location=Dordrecht |oclc=10726931}}</ref> However, this solution was limited to purely Euclidean spaces. In 2011 the solution in <math>\mathbb{R}_{4,1,0}</math> (3DCGA) was published by [[Leo Dorst]] and Robert Jan Valkenburg, and was the first solution in a Lorentzian signature.<ref>{{Citation |last1=Dorst |first1=Leo |chapter=Square Root and Logarithm of Rotors in 3D Conformal Geometric Algebra Using Polar Decomposition |date=2011 |chapter-url=http://link.springer.com/10.1007/978-0-85729-811-9_5 |title=Guide to Geometric Algebra in Practice |pages=81–104 |editor-last=Dorst |editor-first=Leo |place=London |publisher=Springer London |language=en |doi=10.1007/978-0-85729-811-9_5 |isbn=978-0-85729-810-2 |access-date=2021-11-13 |last2=Valkenburg |first2=Robert |editor2-last=Lasenby |editor2-first=Joan|editor2-link=Joan Lasenby}}</ref> Also in 2011, Charles Gunn was the first to give a solution in the degenerate metric <math>\mathbb{R}_{3,0,1}</math>.<ref>{{Cite thesis |last=Gunn |first=Charles |date=19 December 2011 |publisher=Technische Universität Berlin |title=Geometry, Kinematics, and Rigid Body Mechanics in Cayley-Klein Geometries |url=https://depositonce.tu-berlin.de/handle/11303/3355 |language=en |doi=10.14279/DEPOSITONCE-3058}}</ref> This offered a first glimpse that the principle might be metric independent. Then, in 2021, the full metric and dimension independent closed form solution was given by Martin Roelfs in his PhD thesis.<ref>{{Cite thesis |last=Roelfs |first=Martin |date=2021 |title=Spectroscopic and Geometric Algebra Methods for Lattice Gauge Theory |url=http://rgdoi.net/10.13140/RG.2.2.23224.67848 |language=en |doi=10.13140/RG.2.2.23224.67848}}</ref> And because bivectors in a geometric algebra <math>\mathbb{R}_{p,q,r}</math> form the Lie algebra <math>\mathfrak{spin}(p,q,r)</math>, the thesis was also the first to use this to decompose elements of <math>\text{Spin}(p,q,r)</math> groups into orthogonal commuting factors which each follow Euler's formula, and to present closed form exponential and logarithmic functions for these groups. Subsequently, in a paper by Martin Roelfs and Steven De Keninck the invariant decomposition was extended to include elements of <math>\text{Pin}(p,q,r)</math>, not just <math>\text{Spin}(p,q,r)</math>, and the direct decomposition of elements of <math>\text{Spin}(p,q,r)</math> without having to pass through <math>\mathfrak{spin}(p,q,r)</math> was found.<ref name=":0" />
